title: The Gullibility Episode
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro co-host Chuck) explore gullibility: how it differs from credulity, Stephen Greenspan's book "Annals of Gullibility" and his own Madoff loss, the gullibility scale by Alessandra Tanesini of Macquarie University, personality and situational factors (social pressure, expertise, impulsivity, need for independence, cynicism, intuition), childhood trauma research from University of Leicester, mood effects, older adults and scams, romance scams and Monica Whitty's 2018 research, Better Business Bureau data on younger victims, scientists being gullible, trust versus gullibility (Toshio Yamagishi's research and emancipation theory), Hugo Mercier's book "Not Born Yesterday," propaganda and political ads, the Global Anti-Scam Alliance trillion-dollar scam estimate, and tips to avoid being duped. Ends with a listener mail about automat-themed Bach concert from Reverend Mark Oldenburg-Steinmiller.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about Chuck being sick and introduce the topic of gullibility, noting that social psychologists are still studying it.

segments.title: Credulity vs. gullibility definitions
segments.summary: Stephen Greenspan's distinction between credulity and gullibility is introduced, and Josh disagrees with it, arguing that gullibility is believing without checking evidence.

segments.title: Greenspan's four factors and the gullibility scale
segments.summary: Greenspan's factors are described: situational pressure, cognitive issues, lack of expertise, and personality. Greenspan's own Madoff loss is mentioned. A gullibility self-report scale from Macquarie University is described and validated against phishing clicks.

segments.title: Personality, social intelligence, and Madoff
segments.summary: Personality traits such as impulsivity, low curiosity, and high need for independence raise gullibility risk. Social intelligence is discussed as a protective skill, and Greenspan's Madoff loss is reviewed.

segments.title: Parenting, self-confidence, and childhood trauma
segments.summary: Parenting that undermines a child's confidence can make adults more gullible. A University of Leicester study links childhood trauma to later gullibility because it erodes trust in one's own judgment.

segments.title: Intuition and cynicism as vulnerabilities
segments.summary: Relying on intuition and being cynical both raise gullibility. Cynicism is described as a lazy shortcut that makes people easy to manipulate by someone speaking their language.

segments.title: Mood, meals, and older adults
segments.summary: Mood affects susceptibility: good mood via a free lunch (Gregory Razran 1938 study) and low mood increasing attention. Older adults may be vulnerable to cognitive decline but may be protected by constant warnings.

segments.title: Scam victims and the University of Tirana study
segments.summary: A University of Tirana study of adults aged 60 to 90 found that prior fraud victims had lower conscientiousness and honesty-humility. People with cognitive decline were more often targeted, and falling for a scam has been suggested as a reason for dementia testing.

segments.title: Romance scams, catfishing, and young adults
segments.summary: Monica Whitty's 2018 research on romance scams found victims were more impulsive and sensation-seeking, and more highly educated. A Better Business Bureau analysis found 25 to 35 year olds lost more money to scams than older people.

segments.title: Scientists can be gullible
segments.summary: Scientists can be gullible because expertise breeds overconfidence, they may apply field knowledge to other fields, and they want to be right, so they may confirm hypotheses instead of testing them. Fraudulent results are mentioned.

segments.title: Ad break and tangent
segments.summary: Ad break with brief banter about Bill Murray and Lucy Lu jokes.

segments.title: Trust is not the same as gullibility
segments.summary: Toshio Yamagishi's research at Hokkaido University found high-trust and low-trust people scored about the same on gullibility tests. High trust is linked to better discernment. Yamagishi's emancipation theory is discussed.

segments.title: Social connection and trust
segments.summary: Not trusting others carries opportunity costs, and social connection is linked to healthier aging. Trauma or a dismissive upbringing can make people doubt their judgment.

segments.title: Hugo Mercier, propaganda, and political ads
segments.summary: Hugo Mercier's book Not Born Yesterday argues people are less gullible than assumed. Propaganda reinforces existing beliefs rather than creating new ones, and political ads are discussed as ineffective.

segments.title: Scam losses and tips to avoid being duped
segments.summary: The Global Anti-Scam Alliance estimates a trillion dollars lost to scams worldwide each year. The hosts list tips: admit susceptibility, avoid emotional decisions, ask questions, and consider the source.

segments.title: Listener mail: automat Bach concert
segments.summary: Reverend Mark Oldenburg-Steinmiller writes about an automat-themed Bach concert performed with household items found in an automat, and about a 1970 trip to the New York Automat.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and iHeartRadio production note.
